document.title: Motion to Intervene and Request for Clarification of Talen Energy Corporation re the Reliability Backstop Procurement filing

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
Docket No. ER26-3380-000 
 
MOTION TO INTERVENE AND REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF 
TALEN ENERGY CORPORATION 
 
Talen Energy Corporation (“Talen”) hereby submits this motion to intervene and 
respectfully requests the Commission clarify one provision of the Reliability Backstop 
Procurement (“RBP”) filing submitted by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”).  PJM states in its 
transmittal letter that the RBP filing is “not intended to disrupt existing commercial agreements,”1 
which is consistent with the directive from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” 
or “Commission”).  Yet, PJM’s proposal will unequivocally diminish the economic benefit secured 
by new load under previously negotiated contracts for the purchase and sale of capacity from 
existing generation resources.  Accordingly, the Commission should clarify the proposed Tariff 
revisions at Attachment DD, section 18.3(a) to include a reduction to the Electric Distributor’s 
zone/area’s pro-rata allocation of the Initial RBP Target MW equal to the contracted amount of 
large load that has executed a power purchase agreement (“PPA”) or similar supply contract with 
an existing generation resource prior to the January 16, 2026 Statement of Principles.2 
     
 
1  
Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming from Large Loads at 3, 
Docket No. EC26-3380-000 (filed July 31, 2026) (“PJM RBP Filing”). 
2  
Statement of Principles Regarding PJM, NATL. ENERGY DOMINANCE COUNCIL (issued Jan. 16, 2026), available 
at https://www.energy.gov/documents/statement-principles-regarding-pjm.  Talen submits its Request for 
Clarification pursuant to Rule 212 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure.  18 C.F.R. § 385.212 
(2026).

2 
 
I. 
MOTION TO INTERVENE 
Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,3 Talen 
respectfully submits this motion to intervene in the above-captioned proceeding.  The formal legal 
name of Talen is Talen Energy Corporation.  Talen is a corporation organized and existing under 
the laws of Delaware.  Talen maintains its principal place of business at 2929 Allen Parkway, 22nd 
Floor, Houston, Texas 77019. Talen is a leading independent power producer and energy 
infrastructure company which owns and operates approximately 15.7 gigawatts of power 
infrastructure in the United States.  Talen produces and sells electricity, capacity, and ancillary 
services into wholesale U.S. power markets, including and primarily in PJM.  A subsidiary of 
Talen has entered into a bilateral contract for the sale of electric power from an existing generation 
resource to new load that will come online during the Delivery Years set forth in the PJM RBP 
Filing.  Accordingly, the actions taken by the Commission in this matter will directly affect the 
interests of Talen.  Talen has a direct and material interest in the instant proceeding that no other 
party can adequately represent.  Talen therefore requests that the Commission grant this motion to 
intervene and permit Talen to participate in this proceeding with full rights as a party thereto. 
II. 
REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION    
A. 
The proposed Tariff revisions do not protect existing commercial agreements 
from disruption.  
The protection of existing private contracts is fundamental to the operations of state and 
federal government, including FERC.4  The Commission has previously acknowledged that 
“uncertainties regarding rate stability and contract sanctity can have a chilling effect on 
 
3  
18 C.F.R. § 385.214 (2026).  
4  
See, e.g., U.S. Const, Art. I, § 10, clause 1 (setting forth that “[n]o State shall . . . pass any . . . [l]aw impairing the 
[o]bligation of contracts”).

3 
 
investments and a seller’s willingness to enter into long-term contracts and this, in turn, can harm 
customers in the long run.”5  The Commission has also recognized that electric industry innovation 
does not justify injecting uncertainty and upheaval into existing contracts.6   
The past few years have presented historic opportunities and novel challenges.  Although 
all market participants could have benefitted from regulatory certainty during this period, it was 
not an option to wait idly for PJM and the Commission to enact generalized market reform that 
would adequately address the evolving market dynamics and increasing load demand.7  Large load 
developers were faced with three options:  bring their own power, rely on the market, or fix power 
costs through a bilateral PPA.  Speed to power is paramount for new large load customers.  
Accordingly, certain developers chose to fix their costs—or so they thought—by means of a 
bilateral PPA.  These contracts were executed at a time when the RBP was not known to be on the 
horizon.  The PJM RBP Filing, without clarification, treats developers that chose Option No. 3 
(bilateral PPAs) the same as developers that chose Option No. 2 (rely on the market).  Such an 
outcome upsets the reasonable, investment-backed expectations that FERC has historically sought 
to protect.   
The importance of reliance interests and the risk of chilling investment due to regulatory 
instability are not lost on this Commission.  That is why Chairman Laura Swett recently explained 
 
5  
Market–Based Rates for Wholesale Sales of Electric Energy, Capacity and Ancillary Services by Public Utilities, 
Order No. 697, 72 Fed. Reg. 39,904, 119 FERC ¶ 61,295, at P 6 (2007). 
6  
Promoting Wholesale Competition Through Open Access Non-Discriminatory Transmission Services by Public 
Utilities; Recovery of Stranded Costs by Public Utilities and Transmitting Utilities, Order No. 888 at p. 84, 61 
Fed. Reg. 21,540 (May 10, 1996) (“Order No. 888”) (holding that that “changes in the industry have been and 
continue to be dramatic,” but FERC “does not believe they compel generic abrogation of requirements and 
transmission contracts”).  
7  
Delay could also be seen as a national security risk. See generally PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 
61,078 (2024) (Chairman Phillips dissent at P 3) (explaining that “maintaining U.S. leadership in Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) is necessary to maintaining our national security”).

4 
 
that the Commission’s actions with respect to large load reforms and procedures “are not intended 
to disrupt existing commercial agreements.”8  PJM appeared to take note because PJM stated in 
its filing that its proposal “avoids disrupting existing commercial arrangements.”9  However, the 
PJM RBP Filing does not adequately implement this principle and requires further clarification.    
Under proposed Attachment DD, section 18.3(a), each Electric Distributor zone/area’s 
allocation of the Initial RBP Target may be reduced by the quantity of “Qualifying RBP Offset 
UCAP MW” or by an opt-out provision.10  This does not account for new load that has entered 
into a bilateral PPA with an existing generation resource.  As a result, each Electric Distributor 
zone/area will continue to be allocated an inflated share of the Initial RBP Target.  Such new load 
will be subject to RBP Charges, assuming states follow the Commission’s directive to implement 
RBP cost allocation mechanisms.11  Therefore, this “new load” must pay incremental capacity 
charges resulting from the RBP, thereby minimizing the economic benefit the load freely 
negotiated under its fixed-cost, bilateral PPA (essentially, paying twice for capacity).   
 
8  
Statement of FERC Chairman Laura Swett, FERC Open Meeting (June 18, 2026) at 10:42, https://ferc.gov/news-
events/events/june-18-2026-open-meeting-10082025.  
9  
Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.3(a).  Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW means unforced capacity 
that has not received a reliability pricing model commitment or been committed in a Fixed Resource Requirement 
Plan as of the commencement date of the RBP, is supplied by new build or incremental generation that will 
perform based on PJM dispatch instructions by no later than June 1, 2032, and is evidenced by signed bilateral 
contracts, signed commitment letters, or self-supply that is in a relevant electric retail regulatory authority-
approved or accepted integrated resource plan.  See PJM RBP Filing at 35 (citing Proposed Tariff, Attachment 
DD, section 18.2(c)). 
10  Id. at 35 (citing Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.2(c)).  
11  Id. at 96-97 (“PJM is proposing to allocate daily RBP Charges to relevant Electric Distributor zones/areas, pro 
rata, based on the zone/area’s assigned share of the total, region-wide Final RBP Target MW . . . .”).

5 
 
B. 
The Commission should clarify Attachment DD, section 18.3(a) to further 
reduce each Electric Distributor zone/area’s allocation of the Initial RBP 
Target. 
PJM has expressly consented “to the Commission’s exercise of authority to modify and/or 
sever the proposed Tariff and RAA language, as needed and permitted under the FPA and NRG 
Power Marketing, where such modification is consistent with PJM’s overarching objectives in this 
filing.”12  If the Commission exercises its authority to modify the PJM RBP Filing, then PJM 
requested that “the Commission expressly prescribe the revised rate or rule in its order.”13  The 
Commission should do so here.  Specifically, Talen requests that the Commission require the 
following underlined language to Attachment DD, section 18.3(a) in its approval of the PJM RBP 
Filing: 
(a) 
Cost Allocation to Electric Distribution zone/area 
The Office of the Interconnection shall allocate the Initial RBP 
Target MW to each Electric Distributor’s zone/area pro-rata share of 
the difference between the forecasted Load Adjustments for the 
2026/2027 Delivery Year and the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.  
The difference between the forecasted Load Adjustments for the 
2026/2027 and the 2028/2029 Delivery Years shall be reduced for 
the purpose of this calculation to the extent: 
(i) 
an Electric Distributor, LSE, Transmission Owner, 
or other entity provides the Office of Interconnection 
with evidence of Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW, 
in accordance with Tariff, Attachment DD, section 
18.2 and as may be further set forth in the PJM 
Manuals; or  
(ii) 
an Electric Distributor zonee[sic]/area meets one of 
the opt-out provisions set forth in accordance with 
Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.1(d); and 
 
12  Id. at 131 (internal citations omitted). 
13  Id.

6 
 
(iii) 
an Electric Distributor, LSE, Transmission Owner, 
or other entity provides the Office of Interconnection 
with evidence of a bilateral contract executed prior 
to January 16, 2026, for the sale of capacity from an 
existing Generation Capacity Resource to and 
purchased by load under a power purchase 
agreement or similar power supply contract 
indicating that the load will be coming online in the 
2027/2028 or 2028/2029 Delivery Year, for a term of 
at least five Delivery Years with a commercial 
operation date prior to the start of the 2032/2033 
Delivery Year; provided that, such reduction shall be 
equal to the total quantity of capacity to be sold and 
purchased under such bilateral contract during the 
2027/2028 and 2028/2029 Delivery Years.   
The resulting reduced MW, floored at zero, is used to calculate the 
zone/area’s assigned pro-rata share of the Final RBP Target MW.  
The zone/area’s assigned share of the Final RBP Target MW shall 
remain constant throughout the fixed 15-year term.  
The Office of the Interconnection shall allocate the total RBP 
Charges, assessed daily, to an Electric Distributor’s zone/area on a 
pro-rata basis using the zone/area’s assigned share of the total Final 
RBP Target MW across all zones/areas. 
The proposed language would effectively treat capacity procured through previously 
executed bilateral contracts with existing generation resources the same as Qualifying RBP Offset 
UCAP MW for purposes of reducing an Electric Distributor zone/area’s allocation of the Initial 
RBP Target and, as a result, allocation of RBP Charges.  
This clarifying language does not reduce the Initial RBP Target such that capacity contracts 
with existing generation resources would be treated as Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW.14  This 
means that PJM will continue to procure the amount of capacity it has deemed necessary under the 
Initial RBP Target; however, the allocation of RBP Charges would be fairly distributed such that 
new load that has previously contracted for capacity with existing generators under qualifying 
 
14  See Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.2(b).

7 
 
bilateral contracts would not have their previous negotiated economic bargains upset by the PJM 
RBP Filing.  This outcome is consistent with the directive from Chairman Swett to not “disrupt 
existing commercial arrangements.”15 It is also consistent with PJM’s characterization of the PJM 
RBP Filing as revisions that “avoid[] disrupting existing commercial arrangements.”16 
III. 
CONCLUSION  
For the reasons discussed herein, Talen respectfully requests that the Commission clarify 
proposed Attachment DD, section 18.3(a), as discussed above, to bring the language in alignment 
with PJM’s characterization of the PJM RBP Filing and directive from Chairman Swett.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
       Respectfully Submitted, 
 
 /s/ Jennifer Mansh
